headline: Owning the press. Entering the newsroom.
summary: The record includes independent publishing, reporting under threat, press credentials, newsroom training and ownership. Access to a newsroom did not automatically bring authority, safety or equal treatment.
coverageNote: Five episodes centered on U.S. newspapers and White House reporting. These do not establish the history of every broadcast, digital, commentary or local newsroom role.
question: What hiring, credentialing or promotion record connects Black journalists to your actual newsroom?

events.title: Cornish and Russwurm publish an independent Black newspaper
events.people: Samuel E. Cornish, John Brown Russwurm and supporting free Black New Yorkers
events.decisionMaker: Cornish and Russwurm, the newspaper's founders and editors.
events.barrier: White newspapers and literature misrepresented Black Americans, according to the Library of Congress's account.
events.change: Freedom's Journal created a Black-edited outlet for reporting, argument and community information.
events.outcome: It published from 1827 to 1829, carried advertisements for Black businesses and schools, and used subscription agents in the United States and abroad.
events.limit: The publication establishes an independent press institution, not broad entry into white-owned newsrooms; disputes later divided its editors.

source.title: Library of Congress · Freedom's Journal, 1827–1829
source.locator: About this Newspaper; publication dates and historical description

events.title: Ida B. Wells keeps reporting after her newspaper is attacked
events.people: Ida B. Wells and New York Age publisher T. Thomas Fortune
events.decisionMaker: Wells chose to investigate lynching; Fortune's newspaper provided an outlet after a mob destroyed her Memphis equipment.
events.barrier: A white mob attacked her newspaper office, and threats made returning to Memphis dangerous.
events.change: Wells continued the investigation from the North and published an extended account in the New York Age.
events.outcome: Her reporting continued through another Black newspaper, despite the destruction of her own workplace.
events.limit: This is a record of institutional support and survival under violence, not a policy victory that made journalism safe or equally accessible.

source.title: National Park Service · Ida B. Wells
source.locator: Biography paragraphs covering the 1892 lynchings, destruction of her office and New York Age reporting

events.title: Alice Dunnigan gains White House press credentials
events.people: Alice Dunnigan of the Associated Negro Press; later, Ethel Payne of the Chicago Defender
events.decisionMaker: White House press credentialing admitted Dunnigan; the WHCA account does not identify the individual approving official.
events.barrier: The White House Correspondents' Association identifies her as the first Black woman credentialed to report there.
events.change: Dunnigan could bring her news service's reporting and questions into presidential press conferences.
events.outcome: She and Payne pressed President Eisenhower about civil rights; the association records that he eventually stopped calling on them.
events.limit: A credential granted entry, not equal opportunity to question the president or control over a newsroom's hiring.

source.title: White House Correspondents' Association · Honoring Alice Dunnigan and Ethel Payne
source.locator: April 25, 2022; paragraphs on 1947 credentialing and Eisenhower-era press conferences

events.title: Journalists organize training and an institution to sustain it
events.people: Robert C. Maynard and fellow Summer Program for Minority Journalists founders
events.decisionMaker: The program founders established the Institute for Journalism Education in 1977.
events.barrier: The institute's history describes severe underrepresentation in newsrooms and leadership.
events.change: A Berkeley summer training program admitted its first class in 1976; the new institute sustained professional education.
events.outcome: The institute later added editing and newsroom-management programs.
events.limit: Program operation does not establish hiring or promotion at your newsroom.

source.title: Maynard Institute · Our History
source.locator: Our decades of impact: 1976, August 31, 1977, 1980 and 1985 entries

events.title: Robert and Nancy Maynard acquire the Oakland Tribune
events.people: Robert C. Maynard and Nancy Hicks Maynard
events.barrier: Newsroom employment and newspaper ownership are different forms of access.
events.change: The acquisition placed an established daily under Black ownership.
events.outcome: The institute records the completed purchase in 1983.
events.limit: Ownership alone does not establish particular hiring, pay or promotion outcomes.

source.title: Maynard Institute · Our History
source.locator: Our decades of impact: 1983 Oakland Tribune purchase entry
